beats.trigger: ## From Personal to Team
beats.got: nothing new; it's a title, though it's the problem I actually have.

beats.trigger: You can't really share an agent.
beats.got: Sharing means picking one of four things (context, skill, output or interface), and the pick is a strategy call. That is more useful than 'just give everyone access'.

beats.trigger: **Bring one example from your own organisation where people got access to a tool and did not use it.**
beats.got: The module wants a real failed rollout. I have one: the BI portal nobody opened after launch.

beats.trigger: **Test** the switch assumptions and name one person and one test to take out of the room
beats.got: The module ends with one person and one test. I like that it's that concrete, and it isn't fourteen people.

beats.trigger: What would you want a teammate to have: your `memory/` folder, one of your skills, the morning output, or a way to ask the agent a question in Slack? And why that one?
beats.got: The first question forces a choice, and I immediately lean towards sharing the context, because that's what my team lacks.

beats.trigger: The starting question is theirs, not yours: *what job is my teammate trying to get done, and which sharing shape does it?*
beats.got: I should start from my teammate's job, not from what I built. That's the discipline I'd apply to any product decision, but I hadn't applied it to this.

beats.trigger: The test is specificity: does it name one teammate, their current way of doing the job, and an outcome you could observe?
beats.got: The agent interviews me about one teammate, and I check that the result is specific. I'll check it, but I have fourteen people and this only covers one of them.

beats.trigger: If the reason is merely *"we already have the platform,"* send it back.
beats.got: Four sharing options, and 'we already have the platform' isn't an acceptable reason. That is how my own team picks tools, so it's uncomfortable and useful.

beats.trigger: You now have the teammate's job and a candidate selected against it.
beats.got: nothing new; it's a hand-off to the next exercise.

beats.trigger: Now find the obstacle that decides whether the teammate can actually absorb it, then draft both halves of the plan.
beats.got: Next is the obstacle and a plan with two halves. The setup is clear.

beats.trigger: A good bottleneck explains why several other obstacles stay hard.
beats.got: I should look for the one obstacle that keeps the others hard, not list all of them. I'd expect the real one on my team to be that nobody owns the shared context.

beats.trigger: A polished technical file beside a people file full of unnamed roles is the finding, not a finished rollout.
beats.got: The agent won't invent owners for me. Unnamed roles stay visible as Monday's question, so I'd see exactly where my plan is thin.

beats.trigger: [Test the sharing plan](test-the-sharing-plan.md) checks the assumptions underneath these plans, imagines the failure, and writes the first real-world contact to `module-7/monday.md`.
beats.got: nothing new; it's another hand-off.

beats.trigger: The technical and people plans are hypotheses.
beats.got: My plans are hypotheses and I should test them. That's fair, and it's how I'd treat a pricing pilot.

beats.trigger: Use Roger Martin's question: *what would have to be true for this teammate, doing this job, to fire their current hire and use my candidate?*
beats.got: I should ask what would make my teammate drop their current way of working, which makes it feel like a competitive analysis, a frame I'm used to from consulting.

beats.trigger: Six months from now, the teammate went back to the incumbent.
beats.got: I imagine the failure in advance and pick one person, one question and one test for Monday. The premortem is the useful part.

beats.trigger: A candidate picked because it fits the infrastructure is shopping. A candidate picked because it moves the outcome is design.
beats.got: nothing new; this is the 'don't pick on infrastructure' point for the third time. The shopping versus design line is neat, but I already had it.

beats.trigger: ## Lecture: Access is not absorption
beats.got: nothing new; it's a lecture title.

beats.trigger: The two get reported as one number and they are not one thing.
beats.got: A licence count measures access, not absorption, and my dashboards mix the two. It's true, though the point was already made in the Big Idea.

beats.trigger: The proposal got neither a yes nor a no.
beats.got: A good analysis can die when urgency moves on and leadership hasn't done the work themselves. I recognise that from my own CFO conversations. It is someone else's company, but it could have been mine.

beats.trigger: Accountability is the part with a name on it, and a name does not travel inside a folder.
beats.got: Context, boundary and checks copy easily, but accountability doesn't. That explains why the folders my team copies keep going stale.

beats.trigger: Pick the one your teammate's week can take in.
beats.got: Each sharing strategy asks something different of the person receiving it. That mostly restates the earlier pick-against-the-outcome step.

beats.trigger: Somebody they trust has to have used it first and said so.
beats.got: nothing new; this is the switch question again, with the useful addition that a trusted person has to go first.

beats.trigger: Have the conversation before you build anything more.
beats.got: Talk to one person before building anything else. I can do that Monday without anyone's permission.

beats.trigger: Who gets your context, who gets a skill, who wants only the output, and who would use an @mention?
beats.got: Different teammates need different shapes, and I should sort my fourteen people that way. That makes it actionable for the whole team.

beats.trigger: Access is a switch someone flips. Absorption happens in other people's weeks.
beats.got: nothing new; it's a recap of things I've already read.

beats.trigger: Their answer is the evidence. The plan is still the hypothesis.
beats.got: Next time I bring what the person actually said, not my plan, which keeps me honest.

beats.trigger: What if you didn't have to build each one by hand?
beats.got: The next module is about not building every agent by hand. That might help my team, but it's a teaser.

take_homes: Start from the teammate's actual job and what they do today, then choose between sharing context, a skill, the output or an interface. Don't start from what I built.
Copying files doesn't move accountability. Every plan needs a named owner, and the agent leaves the gaps visible when I haven't named one.
Talk to one person before building more, and ask what would have to be true for them to drop their current way of doing it.

monday.move: Ask one teammate how they currently produce the pilot-cohort numbers for the usage-pricing decision, and what would make them switch. Run the module's interview prompt first so I go in with a draft job and a candidate (probably sharing the context). Put one shared place for the context files on the list as the first thing to fix.
monday.who: The analyst on my team who rebuilds the pilot-cohort brief each week (I'll pick the name Monday morning).
monday.when: Monday morning for the conversation. The brief goes to the pricing working group on its usual day if the answer holds up.
monday.stop_condition: If the person says their current way works fine and nothing in my candidate would make them switch, I drop that candidate and don't build it.
monday.blocker: My team has no shared place for the context files and everyone keeps their own copy. I also don't know yet who would own it.

misconception.why: I came in thinking the skill was writing better prompts. The module's point is that sharing fails on ownership and on whether the teammate would switch, which no prompt fixes. I'm not convinced prompts don't matter, since the prompts still did the work in each step. I just see now that they aren't the bottleneck for a team.

one_line: Useful for anyone who has to get a whole team onto this, and it left me with one named person and one question for Monday. It makes the same point about infrastructure about three times.
